title: Pesticide Record-Keeping for Small and Hobby Farms
excerpt: The federal USDA rule for restricted-use pesticide records ended in July 2025, but state rules, product labels and worker-protection requirements still apply. Here is what small and hobby farms should keep, and why good spray records still pay off.
author: FarmVoice Records

sections.heading: Importance of Pesticide Record-Keeping
sections.body: Good spray records protect small and hobby farms in an inspection, an insurance claim or a dispute with a neighbor. They also show what worked: which product, how much, and when. Even where no rule requires a record, writing it down right after you spray is the cheapest insurance a farm can have.

sections.heading: What the Rules Require Now
sections.body: For years, a federal USDA rule (7 CFR Part 110) required certified private applicators to keep restricted-use pesticide (RUP) records for two years. USDA removed that rule effective July 11, 2025. That does not mean records are optional: many states have their own pesticide recordkeeping rules, the product label is the law, and farms with agricultural employees must follow the EPA Worker Protection Standard, which has its own application-information requirements. Check with your state department of agriculture or extension office for what applies to you.

sections.heading: Key Components of a Pesticide Record
sections.body: A useful pesticide record includes the product name and EPA registration number, the amount applied, the date, the field or location and its size, the crop or site, and the name and certification number of the applicator. Many farmers also note the application method, weather and wind at the time, and any problems they saw afterwards. Recording the same details every time keeps your records consistent and easy to check.

sections.heading: Best Practices for Maintaining Records
sections.body: Farmers should establish a systematic approach to record-keeping that includes using digital tools or apps for ease of access and organization. Regularly updating records after each application helps maintain accuracy and completeness. Additionally, farmers should consider creating a dedicated space for storing all pesticide-related documents, ensuring they are easily retrievable during inspections.

sections.heading: FarmVoice Records and Pesticide Tracking
sections.body: FarmVoice Records lets you log a spray application by voice or typing right after it happens, with GPS location captured automatically. It checks each record for the standard fields above and flags anything missing before you save, and you can export your records when an inspector, buyer or insurer asks. FarmVoice does not decide which rules apply to your farm; it helps you keep the records those rules call for.

sections.heading: Training and Education
sections.body: Pesticide rules change, as the 2025 federal update shows. Extension services, state departments of agriculture and pesticide applicator recertification courses are the best way to stay current, and many offer free training for small-scale farmers.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Staying Compliant and Safe
sections.body: Keeping good pesticide records is part of running a responsible farm, whatever its size. Know your state's rules, follow the label, keep consistent records after every application, and use tools that make it quick enough to do in the field.
